description: SpaceVision is a multidisciplinary team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in Tunis. Our mission is to develop an intelligent health monitoring and decision-support system designed to support astronauts during space missions.
summary: SpaceVision is an intelligent health monitoring and decision-support system for astronauts on long-duration missions. Radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment can trigger immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events and behavioral health problems, and on deep-space missions the crew must spot these changes largely on their own. SpaceVision gathers health indicators such as vital signs, sleep, activity and self-reported wellbeing into one picture, learns each astronaut’s personal baseline, and flags meaningful deviations early. Each alert comes with a clear explanation and suggested next steps, so the astronaut can evaluate and act on their health status. A structured report can be shared with the ground medical team when communication allows. The system supports the crew and the flight surgeon, and never replaces medical judgment.
details:
What does it do?
SpaceVision continuously consolidates an astronaut’s health indicators and compares them with that person’s own baseline rather than a population average. It tracks the risk areas named in the challenge: cardiovascular status, immune and physiological stress markers, bone and musculoskeletal health, sleep, and psychological wellbeing. When a trend or deviation appears, the astronaut sees a plain-language alert that explains what changed, which indicators drove it and how confident the system is. They also get suggested actions, such as repeating a measurement, adjusting rest or exercise, or contacting the medical team.

Decision support, not diagnosis
The system is advisory. Alerts and recommendations are grounded in explicit rules and sources, and the astronaut and the medical team make the decisions. Every output is traceable: the system records which data, rules and model versions produced it, so the crew and the ground team can review and challenge it.

Built for autonomy and distance
On deep-space missions, communication with Earth can be delayed or interrupted. The architecture is modular and designed to keep working onboard, then synchronize a structured summary with ground teams once a link is available, so the flight surgeon receives context instead of raw data.

Benefits and intended impact
Earlier detection of health changes, less cognitive load on the crew, better-informed conversations with ground medical teams, and greater crew autonomy on missions where help is far away. The same approach could also support remote and underserved healthcare on Earth.

How it is built
A layered architecture: an astronaut-facing interface, a privacy and access-control layer with audit logging, an orchestration layer that routes each task to the most suitable analysis method, a clinical rules and knowledge layer, and interchangeable model components. Engines can be replaced as better ones appear without rebuilding the system.

What makes it creative
Instead of one monolithic predictor, SpaceVision combines personal baselines, explainable alerts and orchestration of several methods, with the human always in the loop.
